title: Half Shiva, half Parvati
hookLine: a poet bows to a couple joined like a word and its meaning, and a sage learns he can't honor one without the other
carry: Shiva and Shakti: two, and never apart
last: WHO ARE YOU? I AM BRAHMAN.

lines: FIRST: A WORD AND ITS MEANING.
cards: A poet sits down to write a long poem about the kings of Raghu's line, one king after another. And the first thing he writes isn't about any king. It's about a word and its meaning.
The poet is Kalidasa, whose Parvati this path met in the forest not long ago. Before he tells a single story, he bows to a couple. Not a king and queen: Shiva and Parvati.
And he chooses one picture to say how close they are.

teach.b: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Joined like word and meaning, for the sake of understanding word and meaning, I bow to the parents of the world, Parvati and Shiva.
A word without meaning is just noise; a meaning needs a word to carry it. Two, and never apart. That's how close the poet says the god and the goddess are.
A temple story makes the same point with a body.
A sage named Bhringi loved Shiva so single-mindedly that he would circle only Shiva in worship, never Parvati.

teach.h: ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.
teach.b: So, as the story is told, Parvati drew close and became one body with Shiva, half and half. In some tellings Bhringi still tried to squeeze between them. The story's point is plain: you cannot honor one without the other.

That shared body is Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman: on one side Shiva, ash and matted hair; on the other Parvati, earring and silk. It's carved in temples to this day. Here's the teaching.
In Hindu thought, Shiva and Shakti aren't two gods who happen to be married.
Many teachers read them as awareness and power, the still and the moving, neither complete alone. Remember the hymn this path met earlier: without Shakti, Shiva cannot even stir.
Today: a Hindu wife is often called ardhangini, the half of the body. Some people hear that and think it makes her half a person. Ardhanarishvara says the opposite.
Even God, in this picture, is only whole as two.

how: The opening verse of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is learned by students of Sanskrit and recited as an invocation, and images of Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half Parvati, stand in temples dedicated to Shiva.

games.q: what does “shakti as a philosophy” mean?
o: a poet's rule for choosing the right word
a royal family line traced back to the gods
Shiva and Shakti, joined like a word and its meaning

games.q: word and meaning — tap the pairs.
p: a poet who bows before he begins
the lord who is half woman
a wife: half of one shared body

s: Kalidasa's poem opens by bowing to Parvati and Shiva
before a single story, he bows to the parents of the world.
in the Bhringi story, the sage manages to worship Shiva alone
Parvati becomes one body with Shiva. there's no honoring one without the other.
in Ardhanarishvara, Shiva and Parvati share one body
half him, half her, divided down the middle.

games.q: a friend hears a wife called ardhangini, 'half the body', and says it sounds like she's half a person. by Ardhanarishvara, what fits?
o: she's right: the wife is the lesser half.
even Shiva is half Parvati: neither is whole alone.
it's an old word; it means nothing now.
games.why: in Ardhanarishvara, Shiva himself is half Parvati. two, and never apart, like Kalidasa's word and meaning.

practice: Choose one simple word that matters to you, home, mother, peace, a name, and say it once, silently, then watch what arrives with it: a picture, a feeling, a face.
Say it again, slowly, and rest wherever the sound and the sense meet. If you pray, you can choose the name of the goddess, or Shiva, or the name you use for God.

wordCard.voice: Shakti as a philosophy. Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vagartha, word and meaning, joined: Kalidasa's picture of Parvati and Shiva.
